lessons.title: Openings and closings
lessons.tip: The first and last moments matter most. Open with something that wakes the audience up: a question, a short story or a surprising fact. Do not start with “Today I will talk about…” Close by returning to your main message and ending with a clear thought or call to action.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

accepted: Last winter, my bus broke down in the snow, and a stranger changed my mind about people.

activities.prompt: Which closing is strongest?
activities.answer: So the next time you feel tired, protect your sleep. Start tonight.

accepted: So the next time you feel tired, protect your sleep. Start tonight.

lessons.title: Signposts
lessons.tip: Signposts tell the audience where you are going, like road signs. At the start, give a map: “I have three points.” Between points say “My second point is…” At the end say “To sum up…” Signposts help listeners who cannot go back and re-read.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Repeat for rhythm
lessons.tip: A tricolon is a list of three: “Stop, look, listen.” Three feels complete and is easy to remember. Anaphora repeats the same words at the start of sentences: “We will work. We will learn. We will win.” Both build rhythm and make a line memorable.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Contrast and questions
lessons.tip: Antithesis puts opposite ideas side by side: “Easy to say, hard to do.” It makes a point clear and strong. A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for an answer: “Who wouldn’t want a safer street?” It makes the audience think.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings

lessons.title: Pause and stress
lessons.tip: A pause is a tool. Pause before an important word to build attention, and after it to let it sink in. Stress the key word: “We need ACTION” means something different from “WE need action.” Short pauses also give you time to breathe and think.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings

lessons.title: Pace, volume and pitch
lessons.tip: Your voice has three controls: pace (speed), volume (loudness) and pitch (how high or low). A flat voice makes people drift away. Speak a little slower for important points and a little louder for key ideas, and let your pitch fall at the end of a statement to sound sure.
sources: Esenwein and Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915, public domain): delivery, openings and closings
Aristotle, Rhetoric, and Cicero’s five canons (public domain); Silva Rhetoricae (BYU) for device names (concepts only)

lessons.title: Body language
lessons.tip: Your body speaks too. Stand tall with your feet apart. Look at different people for two or three seconds each. Use open hands at chest height for gestures, and move with a purpose, not back and forth. Keep your hands out of your pockets.

lessons.title: Manage your nerves

lessons.title: The rule of three
lessons.tip: Listeners remember about three points. Three is enough to feel complete and short enough to recall. Tell them the plan at the start: “I have three reasons.” Number the points as you go, and finish with a one-line recap. If you have six ideas, group them into three or cut the weakest.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric and Cicero, De Oratore (public-domain translations): arrangement, style and delivery as parts of speaking

lessons.title: Stories and examples
lessons.tip: A fact informs; a story helps people feel. A short story has a person, a problem and a change, and it ends with a point: “That is why I now…” Keep it under a minute and cut details that do not help. Turn big numbers into something you can picture: “Ten thousand steps is about a walk from here to the river and back.”

lessons.title: Write for the ear
lessons.tip: Spoken language is different from written language. Use short sentences and common words. Contractions such as “it’s” and “we’re” sound natural. Repeat the key phrase so it sticks. lessons.tip: Look at people, not at the floor or the slide. Hold one thought and look at one person until it ends, then move to someone else. This feels like talking to individuals, not to a crowd. lessons.title: Recover from mistakes
lessons.tip: Everyone makes mistakes. The audience notices less than you think. If you lose your place, pause and breathe. Look at your notes. Say a bridge sentence such as “Let me say that again.” If you say a wrong fact, correct it calmly: “Sorry, it was 1,500, not 15,000.” Do not apologize for a long time. Keep going: confidence is how you recover, not how you avoid mistakes.

lessons.title: Credibility in the first minute
lessons.tip: Listeners decide quickly whether to trust you. Ethos is the trust you build through competence, goodwill and character. In the first minute show why you can speak on the topic, but briefly: one line of experience, not a résumé. Show goodwill by naming what you share with the audience. Then be consistent: confident claims, honest limits (“I do not know that yet”) and no exaggeration. One caught exaggeration costs more credibility than ten strong claims can earn.

Common speechwriting practice: rhetorical figures, problem-solution structure, ceremonial speaking (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Figures that carry an idea
lessons.tip: Rhetorical figures give shape to ideas. Anaphora repeats the start of lines: “We will not tire, we will not yield.” Antithesis sets opposites side by side: “Ask not what… but what…” Chiasmus reverses a phrase: “Work to live; do not live to work.” A tricolon lists three: “faster, safer, cheaper.” Use a figure to sharpen one key idea, not every sentence. Overdecorated speech sounds false.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric and Cicero, De Oratore (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos, logos and the five canons
Common speechwriting practice: rhetorical figures, problem-solution structure, ceremonial speaking (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Metaphor and concrete images
lessons.tip: Abstract ideas become memorable through images. lessons.title: Structures that move people
lessons.tip: Some structures are designed to persuade. In problem-solution, you show a problem, prove its cause and present your solution. The motivated sequence adds steps: get attention, show the need, satisfy it with your plan, help people visualize the result and call for action. Choose the structure that fits the audience: a skeptical audience needs the problem proved; a friendly audience needs a clear action. Use signposts so listeners know where they are.

Common speechwriting practice: rhetorical figures, problem-solution structure, ceremonial speaking (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Difficult audiences and interruptions
lessons.tip: Interruptions and hostility test your poise. Stay calm and lower, not raise, your voice. Acknowledge the feeling without accepting the attack: “I hear that frustration, and I’d like to answer it.” Answer the real question behind the shout. If the person keeps disrupting, offer a limit: “I’ll take that after the talk so everyone can hear the rest.” Do not mock or argue: the room is watching how you treat people.

Common speechwriting practice: rhetorical figures, problem-solution structure, ceremonial speaking (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Toasts, tributes and keynotes
lessons.tip: Ceremonial speaking has its own rules. A toast is short: say who you honor, tell one specific story or quality, and raise the glass with a clear last line. A tribute names what the person gave to others. A keynote opening should connect the theme to the audience’s lives. Be warm but never cruel; humor should include the honoree, not mock them. Practice the timing: ceremonial speeches are remembered for brevity.

lessons.title: Speak on camera and online
lessons.tip: On camera your face and voice are all there is. Place the camera at eye level and look at the lens when you make a key point. Light your face from the front. Use a slightly more energetic voice than usual, because screens flatten energy. Keep gestures within the frame and slides simple. Test sound first, silence notifications, and plan how to recover if the connection fails: say where you will resume.
